===== R1 =====
⟦R1.S0#2a4e76a8⟧ ⟦R1.S0.P1#2a4e76a8⟧
‹s1›Build a deterministic data pipeline tool in Go called `dpipe`. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›The tool operates as a CLI that reads structured data from CSV files, ‹s2.c2›applies a chain of transformations, ‹s2.c3›and writes results to output files — with every step producing bit-identical output across repeated runs given the same input and configuration.

⟦R1.S1#645e7240⟧ ## Core behaviors

⟦R1.S2#dda81266⟧ ### Ingestion

⟦R1.S2.P1#70bbdcf1⟧
`dpipe ingest --input <path> --schema <path> --output <path>`

⟦R1.S2.P2#398a6a10⟧
‹s1›- Reads a CSV file at `<path>`. The first row is a header.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Validates every row against a JSON schema file. The schema has this structure:
  ```json
  {
    "columns": [
      {"name": "id", "type": "int", "required": true, "unique": true},
      {"name": "value", "type": "float", "required": true, "min": 0, "max": 1000},
      {"name": "label", "type": "string", "required": false, "pattern": "^[A-Z]"},
      {"name": "timestamp", "type": "datetime", "required": true}
    ],
    "primary_key": ["id"]
  }
  ```
  Supported types: `int`, ‹s2.c2›`float`, ‹s2.c3›`string`, ‹s2.c4›`datetime` ‹s2.c5›(RFC 3339 format).

⟦R1.S2.P3#697b6f55⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  Column constraints ‹s1.c2›(all optional):
‹s2›‹s2.c1›  - `unique` ‹s2.c2›(boolean): ‹s2.c3›No two valid rows may have the same value in this column. When a duplicate is encountered ‹s2.c4›(checked in input file order after all other validations pass), ‹s2.c5›the later row is rejected with reason `duplicate value for unique column: <name>`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›  - `min`, ‹s3.c2›`max` ‹s3.c3›(number): ‹s3.c4›For `int` and `float` columns only. Value must be within `[min, max]` inclusive. Rejected rows get reason `value out of range for column <name>: <value>`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›  - `pattern` ‹s4.c2›(string): ‹s4.c3›For `string` columns only. Value must match the Go regular expression. Rejected rows get reason `value does not match pattern for column <name>: <value>`.

⟦R1.S2.P4#89c9ed84⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  Validation order for each row: ‹s1.c2›(1) ‹s1.c3›required/type checks, ‹s1.c4›(2) ‹s1.c5›range checks, ‹s1.c6›(3) ‹s1.c7›pattern checks. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›After all rows pass steps 1-3, ‹s2.c2›uniqueness is checked across valid rows in input file order — the first occurrence is kept, ‹s2.c3›subsequent duplicates are rejected.

⟦R1.S2.P5#e86807c6⟧
‹s1.c1›  `primary_key` is always an array of one or more column names ‹s1.c2›(composite key support).

⟦R1.S2.P6#88d8ed51⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Rows that fail validation are written to `<output>.rejected` ‹s1.c2›(same CSV format, with an appended `rejection_reason` column). ‹s1.c3›Valid rows are written to `<output>` in CSV format.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Output rows are sorted by the primary key columns in declaration order: first by the first primary key column, ‹s2.c2›then by the second, ‹s2.c3›etc. Each column is sorted in ascending order using its declared type ‹s2.c4›(numeric sort for int/float, lexicographic for string, chronological for datetime).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- A SHA-256 checksum of the output file ‹s3.c2›(computed on the raw bytes) ‹s3.c3›is written to `<output>.sha256` as a single hex string followed by a newline.

⟦R1.S3#d66eb59e⟧ ### Transformation

⟦R1.S3.P1#8a0428a9⟧
`dpipe transform --input <path> --recipe <path> --output <path> --seed <uint64>`

⟦R1.S3.P2#5f08913b⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Reads a CSV file with a header row. In typical usage this will be a previously ingested ‹s1.c2›(valid) ‹s1.c3›CSV file, ‹s1.c4›but any headered CSV input is allowed.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Applies transformations defined in a JSON recipe file, ‹s2.c2›in order. Each transformation is an object in an array:
  ```json
  [
    {"op": "filter", "column": "value", "condition": "gt", "threshold": 10.0},
    {"op": "derive", "name": "score", "expression": "value * 2 + 1"},
    {"op": "sample", "fraction": 0.5},
    {"op": "sort", "column": "score", "order": "desc"},
    {"op": "rename", "from": "label", "to": "category"},
    {"op": "drop", "columns": ["timestamp"]},
    {"op": "aggregate", "group_by": ["label"], "aggregations": [
      {"column": "value", "function": "sum", "as": "total_value"},
      {"column": "value", "function": "avg", "as": "avg_value"},
      {"column": "id", "function": "count", "as": "num_items"}
    ]},
    {"op": "join", "right": "other.csv", "on": "id", "type": "left"},
    {"op": "window", "function": "rank", "partition_by": ["label"], "order_by": [{"column": "value", "order": "desc"}], "as": "value_rank"},
    {"op": "pivot", "index": ["id"], "column": "label", "value": "value"},
    {"op": "unpivot", "index": ["id"], "columns": ["q1", "q2", "q3"], "name_to": "quarter", "value_to": "amount"},
    {"op": "fill", "columns": ["value"], "strategy": "forward"}
  ]
  ```
‹s3›- Supported operations:
‹s4›‹s4.c1›  - `filter`: Keep rows where `column` satisfies `condition` against `threshold`. Conditions: `gt`, ‹s4.c2›`gte`, ‹s4.c3›`lt`, ‹s4.c4›`lte`, ‹s4.c5›`eq`, ‹s4.c6›`neq`.
‹s5›  - `derive`: Add a new column computed from an expression over existing numeric columns.

⟦R1.S3.P3#a8cbbd3f⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    **Operator precedence** ‹s1.c2›(lowest to highest):
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    1. `||` ‹s2.c2›(logical OR): ‹s2.c3›returns `1` if either operand is > 0, ‹s2.c4›otherwise `0`
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    2. `&&` ‹s3.c2›(logical AND): ‹s3.c3›returns `1` if both operands are > 0, ‹s3.c4›otherwise `0`
‹s4›‹s4.c1›    3. `==`, `!=` ‹s4.c2›(equality): ‹s4.c3›numeric comparison, ‹s4.c4›returns `1` ‹s4.c5›(true) ‹s4.c6›or `0` ‹s4.c7›(false)
‹s5›‹s5.c1›    4. `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` ‹s5.c2›(relational): ‹s5.c3›numeric comparison, ‹s5.c4›returns `1` or `0`
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    5. `+`, `-` ‹s6.c2›(addition, subtraction)
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    6. `*`, `/`, `%` ‹s7.c2›(multiplication, division, modulo)
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    7. Unary `-` ‹s8.c2›(negation)
‹s9›‹s9.c1›    8. Function calls, ‹s9.c2›parentheses, ‹s9.c3›column references, ‹s9.c4›numeric literals

⟦R1.S3.P4#92fb6c93⟧
‹s1›    Division by zero produces `NaN`. ‹s2›Modulo by zero produces `NaN`. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›Any comparison involving `NaN` ‹s3.c2›(on either side) ‹s3.c3›produces `0`.

⟦R1.S3.P5#9f282270⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    The expression evaluator also supports function calls with parenthesized, ‹s1.c2›comma-separated arguments:
‹s2›    - `abs(x)` — absolute value
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `sqrt(x)` — square root; ‹s3.c2›returns `NaN` for negative input
‹s4›    - `ceil(x)` — smallest integer >= x
‹s5›    - `floor(x)` — largest integer <= x
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    - `round(x, n)` — round x to n decimal places ‹s6.c2›(n is a non-negative integer; half-values round away from zero)
‹s7›    - `pow(x, y)` — x raised to the power y
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    - `log(x)` — natural logarithm; ‹s8.c2›returns `NaN` for non-positive input
‹s9›    - `min(x, y)` — minimum of two values
‹s10›    - `max(x, y)` — maximum of two values
‹s11›‹s11.c1›    - `if(cond, x, y)` — returns x if cond > 0, ‹s11.c2›otherwise returns y
‹s12›‹s12.c1›    - `clamp(x, lo, hi)` — returns lo if x < lo, ‹s12.c2›hi if x > hi, ‹s12.c3›otherwise x
‹s13›‹s13.c1›    - `coalesce(x, y)` — returns x if x is not NaN, ‹s13.c2›otherwise returns y

⟦R1.S3.P6#b8b7141a⟧
    Functions can be nested: `round(sqrt(abs(value)), 2)`.

⟦R1.S3.P7#0f97dc1b⟧
‹s1.c1›    Comparison and logical operators enable inline conditions without `if`: e.g., ‹s1.c2›`(value > 10 && value < 100) * value` yields `value` when in range, ‹s1.c3›`0` otherwise.

⟦R1.S3.P8#17f7eb48⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Formatting: derive results are written using the shortest decimal representation that preserves the computed value, ‹s1.c2›without unnecessary trailing zeros or a trailing decimal point ‹s1.c3›(e.g., `11` not `11.0`, `2.5` not `2.50`). ‹s2›`NaN` is written as the literal string `NaN`.

⟦R1.S3.P9#ade451fd⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  - `sample`: Retain the given fraction of rows. The selection must be deterministic given `--seed`. Use the seed to initialize a deterministic PRNG ‹s1.c2›(use Go's `math/rand` with the given seed). ‹s1.c3›Rows are selected by generating a random float for each row in input order; ‹s1.c4›keep the row if the float is < fraction.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›  - `sort`: Sort rows by the given column. `asc` or `desc`. Ties are broken by the original row order ‹s2.c2›(stable sort).
‹s3›  - `rename`: Rename a column.
‹s4›  - `drop`: Remove the listed columns.
‹s5›  - `aggregate`: Group rows by the `group_by` columns and compute aggregations on each group.
    Supported aggregation functions:
‹s6›    - `sum`: sum of numeric values in the column for this group. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `0` if no numeric values exist.
‹s7›    - `avg`: arithmetic mean of numeric values. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.
‹s8›    - `count`: number of non-empty values in the specified column for this group.
‹s9›    - `min`: minimum numeric value. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.
‹s10›    - `max`: maximum numeric value. Empty/non-numeric values are skipped. Result is `NaN` if no numeric values exist.

⟦R1.S3.P10#62f372a5⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Output columns: the group_by columns ‹s1.c2›(in declaration order), ‹s1.c3›followed by the aggregation result columns ‹s1.c4›(in declaration order, using the `as` name). ‹s2›‹s2.c1›Output rows are sorted by the group_by columns in ascending lexicographic order, ‹s2.c2›comparing left to right. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›Numeric aggregation results are formatted without unnecessary trailing zeros ‹s3.c2›(e.g., `10` not `10.0`, `2.5` not `2.50`).

⟦R1.S3.P11#0ec0df15⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Optional `having` clause: after aggregation results are computed and formatted, ‹s1.c2›filter output rows based on an aggregated column. ‹s2›Example:
‹s3›    ```json
    {"op": "aggregate", "group_by": ["label"], "aggregations": [
      {"column": "value", "function": "sum", "as": "total"}
    ], "having": {"column": "total", "condition": "gt", "threshold": 100}}
    ```
‹s4›‹s4.c1›    The `having` object uses the same condition operators as `filter` ‹s4.c2›(`gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `eq`, `neq`). ‹s5›The `column` must reference one of the `as` names from the aggregations. ‹s6›‹s6.c1›The threshold comparison is numeric ‹s6.c2›(the aggregated result string is parsed as a float). ‹s7›Groups whose aggregated value does not satisfy the condition are excluded from output. ‹s8›‹s8.c1›The `having` clause is applied after sorting — it only removes rows, ‹s8.c2›it does not change the relative order of remaining rows.

⟦R1.S3.P12#f683eb75⟧
‹s1›  - `join`: Join current dataset with another CSV file.
‹s2›    - `right`: path to the other CSV file
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `on`: column name that must exist in both datasets ‹s3.c2›(the join key)
‹s4›    - `type`: `"inner"` or `"left"`
‹s5›      - `inner`: output only rows where the join key value exists in both datasets
‹s6›‹s6.c1›      - `left`: output all rows from the current ‹s6.c2›(left) ‹s6.c3›dataset; ‹s6.c4›for rows where the join key has no match in the right dataset, ‹s6.c5›all right-side columns are filled with empty strings
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    - Output columns: all columns from the left dataset, ‹s7.c2›followed by all columns from the right dataset *except* the join key column ‹s7.c3›(to avoid duplication).
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    - If multiple rows in the right dataset share the same join key, ‹s8.c2›only the first one ‹s8.c3›(by file order) ‹s8.c4›is used.
‹s9›‹s9.c1›    - Output rows preserve the order of the left ‹s9.c2›(current) ‹s9.c3›dataset.
‹s10›‹s10.c1›    - If the join key column does not exist in either dataset, ‹s10.c2›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: join key <name> not found in <left|right> dataset`.

⟦R1.S3.P13#81ee37a3⟧
‹s1›  - `window`: Add a new column computed by a window function over partitions of the data.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - `partition_by` ‹s2.c2›(optional): ‹s2.c3›array of column names to partition by. If omitted or empty, ‹s2.c4›all rows are in one partition.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `order_by`: array of ordering specifications, ‹s3.c2›each an object with `"column"` ‹s3.c3›(string) ‹s3.c4›and `"order"` ‹s3.c5›(`"asc"` or `"desc"`). ‹s3.c6›Rows within each partition are ordered by these columns ‹s3.c7›(first column is primary, etc.). ‹s3.c8›Ties in all order_by columns are broken by input row order.
‹s4›    - `as`: name of the new column to create.

⟦R1.S3.P14#1b600a68⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Supported window functions ‹s1.c2›(specified in the `"function"` field):
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - `rank`: 1-based rank within the partition. Rows with equal values in all `order_by` columns receive the same rank. The next rank after a group of ties skips ahead by the group size ‹s2.c2›(e.g., two rows tied at rank 1 → next rank is 3).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `dense_rank`: Like `rank` but without gaps ‹s3.c2›(e.g., two rows tied at rank 1 → next rank is 2).
‹s4›    - `row_number`: Unique sequential number starting from 1 within the partition. Ties are broken by input row order.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›    - `lag`: Value of a source column from a preceding row in partition order. Additional operation fields: `"source_column"` ‹s5.c2›(string), ‹s5.c3›`"offset"` ‹s5.c4›(positive integer, number of rows back), ‹s5.c5›`"default"` ‹s5.c6›(string, value to use when no preceding row exists at that offset). ‹s5.c7›Example:
      ```json
      {"op": "window", "function": "lag", "source_column": "value", "offset": 1, "default": "0", "partition_by": ["cat"], "order_by": [{"column": "id", "order": "asc"}], "as": "prev_value"}
      ```
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    - `lead`: Like `lag` but looks forward ‹s6.c2›(rows ahead in partition order). ‹s6.c3›Same additional fields as `lag`.
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    - `running_sum`: Cumulative sum of a source column's values up to and including the current row within the partition ‹s7.c2›(in partition order). ‹s7.c3›Additional field: `"source_column"`. Non-numeric values are treated as 0. Example:
      ```json
      {"op": "window", "function": "running_sum", "source_column": "value", "partition_by": ["cat"], "order_by": [{"column": "id", "order": "asc"}], "as": "cum_value"}
      ```
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    - `running_avg`: Cumulative average of a source column's numeric values up to and including the current row. Additional field: `"source_column"`. Non-numeric values are skipped from both numerator and denominator. If no numeric values exist up to the current row, ‹s8.c2›the result is `NaN`.
‹s9›‹s9.c1›    - `ntile`: Divide the partition into `n` roughly equal groups numbered 1 through `n`. Additional field: `"n"` ‹s9.c2›(positive integer). ‹s9.c3›If the partition has `k` rows, ‹s9.c4›the first `k mod n` groups have `ceil(k/n)` rows each, ‹s9.c5›and the remaining groups have `floor(k/n)` rows each. Example:
      ```json
      {"op": "window", "function": "ntile", "n": 4, "partition_by": [], "order_by": [{"column": "id", "order": "asc"}], "as": "quartile"}
      ```

⟦R1.S3.P15#0b65801e⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Output: all original columns in their original order, ‹s1.c2›plus the new column appended. ‹s2›‹s2.c1›Output rows preserve the original input row order ‹s2.c2›(not the partition order).

⟦R1.S3.P16#5b56d2d3⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›    Formatting: `rank`, ‹s1.c2›`dense_rank`, ‹s1.c3›`row_number`, ‹s1.c4›and `ntile` results are formatted as integers ‹s1.c5›(no decimal point). ‹s2›‹s2.c1›`running_sum`, ‹s2.c2›`running_avg`, ‹s2.c3›`lag`, ‹s2.c4›and `lead` results are formatted without unnecessary trailing zeros.

⟦R1.S3.P17#577f7453⟧
‹s1.c1›    If any referenced column ‹s1.c2›(in `partition_by`, `order_by`, or `source_column`) ‹s1.c3›does not exist, ‹s1.c4›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.

⟦R1.S3.P18#077cce58⟧
‹s1›  - `pivot`: Reshape data from long format to wide format.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - `index`: array of column names that identify each output row ‹s2.c2›(the row keys).
‹s3›    - `column`: the column whose unique values become new column headers.
‹s4›    - `value`: the column whose values fill the cells.

⟦R1.S3.P19#c21ad861⟧
‹s1›    Behavior:
‹s2›    - Output rows are identified by the unique combinations of `index` column values.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - For each unique value found in `column`, ‹s3.c2›a new output column is created with that value as its header.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›    - The cell at a given ‹s4.c2›(index combination, column value) ‹s4.c3›is filled with the `value` from the first matching input row ‹s4.c4›(by input order) ‹s4.c5›that has that index combination and that column value.
‹s5›‹s5.c1›    - Missing combinations ‹s5.c2›(an index combination that has no row with a particular column value) ‹s5.c3›are filled with empty string.
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    - Output columns: `index` columns ‹s6.c2›(in declaration order), ‹s6.c3›followed by the new pivot columns sorted in ascending lexicographic order.
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    - Output rows are sorted by the `index` columns in ascending lexicographic order, ‹s7.c2›comparing left to right.
‹s8›‹s8.c1›    - If any referenced column ‹s8.c2›(`index`, `column`, or `value`) ‹s8.c3›does not exist, ‹s8.c4›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.

⟦R1.S3.P20#cd122b3d⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›  - `unpivot`: Reshape data from wide format to long format ‹s1.c2›(reverse of pivot).
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - `index`: array of column names to keep as-is ‹s2.c2›(the row identifiers).
‹s3›    - `columns`: array of column names to "melt" into rows.
‹s4›    - `name_to`: name of the new column that will contain the original column names.
‹s5›    - `value_to`: name of the new column that will contain the values.

⟦R1.S3.P21#6ee6b77c⟧
‹s1›    Behavior:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - For each input row, ‹s2.c2›produces one output row per column listed in `columns`.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - Output columns: `index` columns ‹s3.c2›(in declaration order), ‹s3.c3›then `name_to`, ‹s3.c4›then `value_to`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›    - Output rows: for each input row ‹s4.c2›(in original input order), ‹s4.c3›one output row per melted column ‹s4.c4›(in `columns` declaration order).
‹s5›‹s5.c1›    - Empty values are preserved ‹s5.c2›(not skipped).
‹s6›‹s6.c1›    - If any referenced column ‹s6.c2›(in `index` or `columns`) ‹s6.c3›does not exist, ‹s6.c4›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.

⟦R1.S3.P22#efa62a05⟧
‹s1›  - `fill`: Fill empty values in specified columns.
‹s2›    - `columns`: array of column names whose empty values should be filled.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `strategy`: one of `"forward"`, ‹s3.c2›`"backward"`, ‹s3.c3›`"constant"`.
‹s4›‹s4.c1›    - `value` ‹s4.c2›(required only for `"constant"` strategy): ‹s4.c3›the replacement value string.

⟦R1.S3.P23#d7997d65⟧
‹s1›    Behavior:
‹s2›‹s2.c1›    - `"forward"`: scan rows top to bottom. For each specified column, ‹s2.c2›replace each empty value with the most recent non-empty value seen above it in the same column. Leading empty values ‹s2.c3›(no non-empty value above) ‹s2.c4›remain empty.
‹s3›‹s3.c1›    - `"backward"`: scan rows bottom to top. For each specified column, ‹s3.c2›replace each empty value with the nearest non-empty value below it in the same column. Trailing empty values ‹s3.c3›(no non-empty value below) ‹s3.c4›remain empty.
‹s4›    - `"constant"`: replace all empty values in the specified columns with the given `value` string.
‹s5›    - Non-empty values are never modified.
‹s6›    - Output preserves the original row order and all columns.
‹s7›‹s7.c1›    - If any referenced column does not exist, ‹s7.c2›exit with error: `ERROR: invalid recipe: column <name> not found`.

⟦R1.S3.P24#ddc5b7da⟧
‹s1.c1›- After all transformations, ‹s1.c2›write the result CSV to `<output>`, ‹s1.c3›its SHA-256 to `<output>.sha256`.

⟦R1.S4#a6241442⟧ ### Verification

⟦R1.S4.P1#e490b901⟧
`dpipe verify --file <path> --checksum <path>`

⟦R1.S4.P2#06ce0972⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Reads `<path>`, ‹s1.c2›computes SHA-256, ‹s1.c3›compares against the hex string in `<checksum>`.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Exit code 0 and prints `VERIFIED` to stdout if they match; ‹s2.c2›exit code 1 and prints `MISMATCH expected=<expected> actual=<actual>` if they differ.

⟦R1.S5#9d611406⟧ ### Manifest

⟦R1.S5.P1#684e200e⟧
`dpipe manifest --dir <path> --output <path>`

⟦R1.S5.P2#1b2d9453⟧
‹s1›- Recursively scans `<dir>` for all `.csv` files.
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- For each file, ‹s2.c2›computes its SHA-256.
‹s3›- Writes a JSON manifest to `<output>`:
  ```json
  {
    "generated_at": "<RFC 3339 UTC timestamp>",
    "files": [
      {"path": "relative/to/dir/file.csv", "sha256": "abcdef...", "rows": 42, "size_bytes": 1234}
    ]
  }
  ```
‹s4›- The `files` array is sorted by `path` lexicographically.
‹s5›- The `generated_at` timestamp must reflect the actual time of generation.

⟦R1.S6#4dbb6153⟧ ### Pipeline

⟦R1.S6.P1#ad291419⟧
`dpipe pipeline --config <path>`

⟦R1.S6.P2#07799fdd⟧
‹s1›‹s1.c1›- Reads a pipeline config ‹s1.c2›(JSON):
  ‹s1.c3›```json
  {
    "seed": 12345,
    "steps": [
      {"type": "ingest", "input": "raw.csv", "schema": "schema.json", "output": "clean.csv"},
      {"type": "transform", "input": "clean.csv", "recipe": "recipe.json", "output": "final.csv"},
      {"type": "verify", "file": "final.csv", "checksum": "final.csv.sha256"},
      {"type": "manifest", "dir": ".", "output": "manifest.json"}
    ]
  }
  ```
‹s2›‹s2.c1›- Executes each step sequentially. If any step fails, ‹s2.c2›the pipeline stops and exits with code 1, ‹s2.c3›printing `PIPELINE FAILED at step N: <error>` ‹s2.c4›(N is 1-indexed).
‹s3›‹s3.c1›- On success, ‹s3.c2›exits with code 0 and prints `PIPELINE OK: N steps completed`.

⟦R1.S7.P1#36e8fed5⟧
‹s1›Running the same command with the same inputs and seed must always produce byte-identical output files. ‹s2›This applies to all commands. ‹s3›‹s3.c1›The only exception is `generated_at` in manifest output, ‹s3.c2›which reflects wall-clock time.
